title: Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus H5N1 infection in stranded porpoises and dolphins in Chile

analysis.scope_and_question: The study investigates the potential association between HPAIV H5N1 outbreaks and increased cetacean strandings in Chile, focusing on the role of avian influenza A viruses in marine mammals. The central question is whether HPAIV H5N1 is involved in the observed mortality and stranding events among marine birds and pinnipeds.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is based on a survey initiated by the Chilean Fisheries and Aquaculture Service (SERNAPESCA) to document cetacean strandings and assess the presence of HPAIV H5N1 via molecular analysis of swab samples. The evidence includes data on stranding events, molecular testing results, and necropsy findings.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that HPAIV H5N1 was detected in four cetaceans through external swabs and one through internal organs, suggesting a possible link between the virus and cetacean strandings. However, the pathogenic role of the virus in cetaceans remains inconclusive due to limited necropsy data.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review notes that the pathogenic role of HPAIV H5N1 in cetaceans is not definitively established, as only a limited number of necropsies were performed. Additionally, the association between cetacean strandings and HPAIV H5N1 outbreaks is not fully confirmed, highlighting the need for more comprehensive studies.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings suggest the need for further investigation into the role of HPAIV H5N1 in cetacean strandings and mortality. This includes expanding necropsy efforts, enhancing surveillance, and exploring the mechanisms of viral transmission to marine mammals.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the potential link between HPAIV H5N1 outbreaks and increased cetacean strandings in Chile. Between 2022 and 2023, a notable rise in marine bird and pinniped mortality was observed, prompting a survey by SERNAPESCA to assess HPAIV H5N1 presence in cetaceans. In 2023, 205 stranding events involving 281 individuals were recorded, with four cetaceans testing positive for HPAIV H5N1 through swabs and one through necropsy. Histopathological findings were consistent with HPAIV H5N1 infection, though immunohistochemistry was negative. The review highlights the inconclusive role of the virus in cetacean mortality and calls for further research to clarify its impact and transmission mechanisms.

title: Variable transmission efficiency of mammalian origin HPAI D1.1 H5N1 strains in ferrets

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the transmission efficiency of mammalian-origin HPAI D1.1 H5N1 strains in ferrets, as these strains have been increasingly detected in wild bird populations and have spilled over into dairy cattle. The research sought to understand the potential zoonotic risk and transmission dynamics of these strains.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved direct-contact transmission experiments conducted with three distinct D1.1 H5N1 strains in ferrets. Two of the strains were isolated from human infections, while the third was obtained from a lethal cat infection.
analysis.methods: Transmission experiments were performed using direct contact between ferrets to assess the ability of the D1.1 H5N1 strains to spread. The strains were tested in a controlled setting to determine their transmission fitness.
analysis.main_results: Only one human isolate, A/NV/10/2025, was found to transmit efficiently between ferrets. The other strains, including the lethal cat isolate, did not demonstrate efficient transmission.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the mammalian adaptive PB2 D701N mutation may enhance transmission efficiency in D1.1 H5N1 strains, distinguishing them from the PB2 E627K substitution present in the cat isolate.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the importance of monitoring specific mutations in HPAI D1.1 strains for their potential to increase transmission efficiency, which has implications for zoonotic surveillance and risk assessment.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to ferret models and does not account for other potential hosts or environmental factors. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on controlled experimental conditions rather than real-world data.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the transmission efficiency of mammalian-origin HPAI D1.1 H5N1 strains in ferrets, as these strains have been increasingly detected in wild bird populations and have spilled over into dairy cattle. The research aimed to understand the potential zoonotic risk and transmission dynamics of these strains. Three distinct D1.1 H5N1 strains were tested in direct-contact transmission experiments, with two isolated from human infections and one from a lethal cat infection. Only one human isolate, A/NV/10/2025, was found to transmit efficiently between ferrets, while the others did not. The isolate that transmitted efficiently harbored the mammalian adaptive PB2 D701N mutation, suggesting this mutation may contribute to enhanced transmission efficiency in D1.1 strains compared to the PB2 E627K substitution in the cat isolate. The study concludes that the transmission fitness of D1.1 strains is modest, but the emergence of specific mutations at the PB2 701 position warrants special attention. The findings have implications for zoonotic surveillance and risk assessment, emphasizing the need to monitor mutations that may enhance transmission. However, the study is limited to ferret models and does not account for other hosts or environmental factors, which may affect the generalizability of the results.

title: Co-circulation of H5N1 and H5N6 High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza Viruses in Migratory Birds at a Coastal Wintering Site in China

analysis.research_question_and_background: Since 2020, H5Nx high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) belonging to hemagglutinin (HA) clade 2.3.4.4b have undergone widespread dispersal in wild birds, posing substantial threats to global poultry populations and mammals worldwide.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In this study, we report the co-circulation of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 and H5N6 HPAIVs associated with mortality events in Anseriformes and Charadriiformes at a coastal wintering site in Fujian Province, China.
analysis.methods: H5N1 and H5N6 viruses were identified in 4 species of waterfowl (Bean Goose, Eastern Spot-billed Duck, Eurasian Wigeon, and Eurasian Curlew).
analysis.main_results: Phylogenetic analysis indicated that these H5N1 and H5N6 isolates were clade 2.3.4.4b strains circulating within Eurasia and lacked known mammalian adaptation markers in key proteins.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The infected birds exhibited severe systemic multi-organ pathology, with the most pronounced damage observed in the lungs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: H5N6 and H5N1 viruses caused lethal injury in BALB/c mice, with H5N1 leading to systemic infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Environmental sampling also revealed the presence of H5N1 HPAIVs alongside low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) such as H3N1 and H6N1.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the co-circulation of H5N1 and H5N6 high pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (HPAIVs) in migratory birds at a coastal wintering site in Fujian Province, China. The research highlights the presence of these viruses in four waterfowl species and their phylogenetic relationship to strains circulating in Eurasia. The study also reports severe multi-organ pathology in infected birds, with the lungs showing the most damage. Additionally, H5N1 and H5N6 viruses were found to cause lethal injury in BALB/c mice, with H5N1 leading to systemic infection. Environmental sampling further showed the coexistence of H5N1 HPAIVs with low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses. The findings emphasize the dynamic transmission patterns of H5 HPAIVs in wild bird populations and their potential threat to mammals, underscoring the need for sustained surveillance. However, the study's results are limited to the observed environmental and pathological data, and the evidence strength is moderate due to the absence of broader comparative or causal analysis.

title: Mammalian H5N1 cases predict online discourse volume and emotion during the 2024–2025 H5N1 outbreak

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how public perception of H5N1 outbreaks influenced risk communication, as the surge of highly pathogenic avian influenza A (H5N1) infection in animals across the United States since 2024 has renewed pandemic concern.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed 42,957 Reddit comments from January 2024 to December 2025 to characterize online discourse patterns during the H5N1 outbreak.
analysis.methods: Topic modeling was used to identify themes in the online discourse, while sentiment analysis was conducted to determine emotional responses. ARIMAX models with blocked cross-validation were employed to forecast weekly Reddit engagement based on reported cases.
analysis.main_results: Sentiment analysis revealed fear as the dominant emotional response, with anger being the most event-reactive. Reported cases in cats, poultry, and wild mammals correlated with anger. ARIMAX models identified domestic cat and dairy cattle cases as predictors of weekly Reddit engagement, reducing forecasting error by 31% over baseline.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that mammalian cases of H5N1 are associated with early-warning signals for public reaction, providing a one-week window for proactive risk communication.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results offer insights into using online discourse as a tool for monitoring public reaction to H5N1 outbreaks, which can inform more effective risk communication strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on online data, which may not fully represent public sentiment. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the use of a single data source and potential biases in social media engagement.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the relationship between mammalian H5N1 cases and public perception during the 2024–2025 outbreak. By analyzing 42,957 Reddit comments, the researchers identified fear as the dominant emotional response and anger as the most event-reactive. They found that reported cases in cats, poultry, and wild mammals correlated with anger, while ARIMAX models with blocked cross-validation showed that domestic cat and dairy cattle cases predicted weekly Reddit engagement, reducing forecasting error by 31%. The study suggests that mammalian cases can serve as early-warning signals for public reaction, offering a one-week window for proactive risk communication. However, the reliance on online data introduces potential biases, limiting the strength of the evidence. The findings have implications for monitoring public sentiment and improving risk communication strategies during H5N1 outbreaks.

title: Genetic modification of primary airway epithelial cell cultures defines MX1 as a barrier for zoonotic influenza A viruses in the human respiratory epithelium

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of MX1 in restricting zoonotic influenza A viruses in the human respiratory epithelium, addressing the need to understand species barriers that hinder viral transmission.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used primary human airway epithelial cell (hAEC) cultures, including airway organoids and air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures, to model virus-host interactions in the human airway epithelium, which is the primary site of IAV replication.
analysis.methods: The researchers employed engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs) to deliver Cas9-sgRNA ribonucleoprotein complexes into primary hAECs, enabling disruption of MX1 expression and generating MX1-knockout cultures with high genomic-level editing efficiency.
analysis.main_results: MX1 knockout in hAEC ALI cultures had only a minor effect on the replication of the human-adapted H1N1pdm09 strain, but markedly impaired interferon lambda-mediated restriction of zoonotic bovine H5N1/Texas and avian H7N9/Anhui strains, leading to viral titers up to 3-4 logs TCID50 higher than in MX1-competent cultures.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings provide direct evidence that MX1 restricts zoonotic IAVs in primary human airway epithelium, establishing a biologically relevant platform for assessing the sensitivity of emerging IAVs to host factors and their zoonotic and pandemic risk.

title: Rapid UAV-based detection of crane (Grus grus) mortality hotspots during an H5N1 avian influenza outbreak using deep learning

analysis.research_question_and_background: Rapid detection of wildlife mortality during infectious disease outbreaks is essential for ecological risk mitigation, zoonotic-risk management, and timely intervention, yet field surveys are often slow, labor-intensive, and spatially limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study evaluates unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery combined with deep learning as an operational surveillance tool for mapping live and deceased Common Cranes (Grus grus) during a highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) outbreak in the Hula Valley, Israel.
analysis.methods: High-resolution RGB imagery was collected over aquatic roosting and terrestrial feeding habitats and annotated to distinguish living and dead individuals. A YOLOv8-based detection framework was tested using habitat-specific training, combined multi-habitat training, and transfer learning from a large avian dataset, together with selective data augmentation, sliding-window inference, and Weighted Boxes Fusion.
analysis.main_results: Living cranes were detected reliably across habitats, with AP@50 reaching 0.89 in mosaicked feeding-area imagery and 0.98 in raw feeding-area imagery. Dead cranes were detected accurately in water bodies (AP@50 ≈ 0.90), but detection in terrestrial feeding areas remained more limited (AP@50 ≈ 0.64–0.70), based on aerial annotations without in situ confirmation.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings demonstrate the value of UAV-based deep learning for rapid mortality assessment and hotspot identification during wildlife disease outbreaks.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of rapid, scalable surveillance methods for monitoring wildlife mortality during avian influenza outbreaks, aiding in ecological risk mitigation and zoonotic-risk management.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Oversampling, undersampling, and focal loss provided limited improvement, suggesting that class imbalance alone does not fully explain the lower terrestrial detection performance, and that carcass scarcity, limited visual diversity, and ambiguity against heterogeneous ground backgrounds may also contribute.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the use of UAV-based deep learning for rapid detection of Common Crane mortality during an H5N1 avian influenza outbreak in the Hula Valley, Israel. The research highlights the importance of efficient surveillance methods in managing ecological and zoonotic risks. High-resolution RGB imagery was collected and annotated to distinguish living and dead individuals, with a YOLOv8-based framework tested using habitat-specific training, transfer learning, and data augmentation. The results showed reliable detection of living cranes across habitats, with high AP@50 scores, while detection of dead cranes in terrestrial areas was less accurate. The study suggests that UAV-based deep learning can be a valuable tool for identifying mortality hotspots during wildlife disease outbreaks, though limitations in terrestrial detection performance were noted due to factors like carcass scarcity and visual ambiguity. The findings have implications for improving surveillance strategies in avian influenza outbreaks.

title: Highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza infection and exposure in waterfowl and waterbirds of the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge Complex, 2022-2025

analysis.research_question_and_background: The introduction of clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 into North America in 2021 represented a significant shift in disease dynamics for wild waterfowl, creating a need to assess infection and seroprevalence trends after this incursion (A1, A2).
analysis.study_design_and_population: We conducted a surveillance study at the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge Complex from October 2022 to July 2025, sampling 384 swab and 204 sera specimens from assorted waterfowl and waterbird species (A2, A3).
analysis.methods: Samples were collected via swabs and sera from waterfowl and waterbirds, and HPAI H5N1 infection was confirmed by molecular testing of swabs, while serologic testing for H5 and N1 antibodies was performed on sera to assess prior exposure (A3, A4, A5).
analysis.main_results: HPAI H5N1 infection was confirmed in three individuals (two Snow Geese and one Greater White‐fronted Goose) with no symptoms at capture, and antibodies to IAVs were detected in all duck and goose species, with most positives also positive for H5 and N1 antibodies, indicating high prior exposure (A4, A5).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors note that American Coot exhibited lower susceptibility or exposure compared to sympatric waterfowl, and this study reports the first detection of H5 antibodies in American Coot, highlighting the value of serologic surveillance for informing management of HPAI H5N1 risk (A6, A7, A8).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings support using serologic surveillance to monitor HPAI H5N1 risk in wild birds and suggest that widespread prior exposure may reduce susceptibility in some species, informing surveillance and management strategies (A5, A8).
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Although only three infections were detected and American Coot serology was not fully assessed, the large sample size and E1 evidence level provide high confidence in the overall findings (A4, A6).

analysis.summary_en: Following the 2021 emergence of clade 2.3.4.4b highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 in North America, which altered disease dynamics in wild waterfowl, this surveillance study was conducted at the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge Complex from October 2022 to July 2025 to evaluate infection and seroprevalence trends. Researchers collected 384 swab and 204 serum specimens from assorted waterfowl and waterbird species, confirming HPAI H5N1 infection in three asymptomatic individuals (two Snow Geese and one Greater White‐fronted Goose) and detecting influenza A virus antibodies in all duck and goose species, with most positives also positive for H5 and N1 antibodies, indicating high prior exposure. The first detection of H5 antibodies in American Coot was reported, though overall seroprevalence and H5‐specific antibodies were lower than in sympatric waterfowl, suggesting reduced susceptibility or limited exposure. These results underscore the utility of serologic surveillance as a complementary strategy for informing HPAI H5N1 risk management in wild bird populations.

title: Rethinking avian influenza control: a systems-oriented One Health perspective for family poultry

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on avian influenza A viruses, specifically examining the challenges of early detection and control of high- and low-pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI, LPAI) in family poultry systems. It addresses the structural, epidemiological, and socio-economic factors influencing prevention and control, with an emphasis on improving poultry productivity and incorporating smallholder knowledge and participation.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a policy-oriented rapid review that synthesized 110 peer-reviewed publications and 27 policy and guidance documents. It analyzed the structural, epidemiological, and socio-economic factors influencing HPAI and LPAI prevention and control in family poultry systems, with a focus on the lived experiences of poultry keepers and the need for participatory approaches.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: There is consensus that effective HPAI and LPAI control must be embedded within a broader, systems-oriented strategy that improves overall poultry productivity and values smallholder knowledge and participation. Additionally, a multi-hazard risk management approach grounded in One Health is necessary to address equity, food and nutrition security, livelihoods, climate resilience, and global health.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: High background mortality from enzootic diseases such as Newcastle disease and infectious bursal disease obscures recognition of unusual disease events and delays reporting. There is also a need to rebuild trust among family poultry producers, particularly those affected by uncompensated culling during previous HPAI outbreaks.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Locally grounded, participatory approaches that recognize the lived experience of both women and men poultry keepers are required to strengthen surveillance, reporting, and response. Functional cross-sectoral collaboration between public health, animal health, and environmental sectors, along with local government, is essential for effective One Health approaches.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the challenges of controlling avian influenza A viruses, particularly high- and low-pathogenicity strains, in family poultry systems. It emphasizes the need for a systems-oriented approach that integrates structural, epidemiological, and socio-economic factors. The review highlights the importance of participatory methods, trust-building among poultry keepers, and cross-sectoral collaboration to enhance surveillance and response. Despite the synthesis of 110 peer-reviewed publications and 27 policy documents, gaps remain in addressing high background mortality and ensuring equitable participation in control efforts.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1, which has caused severe disease in poultry since 1996, has become panzootic in wild birds and recently has spread to dairy cattle and other mammalian species in the United States.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focuses on the current situation of HPAI H5N1 in Missouri, examining its spread to poultry, wild birds, and some mammals.
analysis.methods: The study relies on surveillance data, outbreak reports, and observations of HPAI H5N1 spread in Missouri, including its presence in poultry, wild birds, and some mammals.
analysis.main_results: Although few human cases have been reported, devastating HPAI H5N1 poultry outbreaks and massive dieoffs in wild birds and in some mammals raise concern about pandemic potential.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as indicating a growing concern for pandemic potential due to the spread of HPAI H5N1 to various animal species, highlighting the need for increased vigilance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the importance of surveillance, early detection, and public health interventions to mitigate the risk of a future HPAI H5N1 pandemic.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on observational data and does not include detailed statistical analysis, which may limit the strength of the evidence regarding pandemic potential.

The authors emphasize the importance of surveillance, early detection, and public health interventions to reduce the risk of a future HPAI H5N1 pandemic. However, the study is based on observational data without detailed statistical analysis, which may limit the strength of the evidence. The findings suggest that farm biosecurity measures and next-generation vaccines could play a critical role in preventing the spread of HPAI H5N1 to humans.

title: Dairy producers' perceptions of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 and their influence on implementation of biosecurity changes

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study was needed due to the challenges posed by the emergence of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in dairy cattle, requiring biosecurity decisions with limited information while balancing evolving guidance, existing beliefs, and farm management constraints.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study aimed to describe dairy producers’ perceptions and understanding of HPAI, characterize experiences and perceived influence among producers affected by HPAI, identify farm characteristics associated with implementation of biosecurity changes in response to HPAI risk, and assess whether perceived biosecurity effectiveness was associated with implementation of biosecurity changes. A questionnaire mailed to Michigan dairy facilities yielded a 15.6% response rate (n = 120/766).
analysis.methods: Descriptive statistics, modified Poisson regression, logistic regression, and parallel mediation analysis using parametric g-computation were used to evaluate survey responses and associations with implementation of biosecurity changes.
analysis.main_results: Overall, 18 respondents (15%) reported confirmed or suspected HPAI on their farms. Among farms without reported confirmed or suspected HPAI, farms with ≥15 employees were more likely to report implementing biosecurity changes than farms with <5 employees (risk ratio [RR] = 2.26; 95% CI: 1.24–4.10), and farms using robotic milking systems were more likely to report changes than farms using parlor or rotary systems (RR = 2.07; 95% CI: 1.21–3.55). From a mediation analysis (n = 93), the estimated probability of implementing biosecurity changes was 45.7% among producers who perceived biosecurity as effective, compared with 21.4% among those who did not, corresponding to a 24.3 percentage-point difference (95% CI: 5.4–42.4).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that implementation of biosecurity changes may be supported by trusted communication strategies that emphasize the effectiveness of specific biosecurity practices and present the disease as a relevant but still manageable farm-level threat.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform the development of targeted communication strategies to improve biosecurity practices among dairy producers, particularly by aligning their perceptions with evidence-supported transmission pathways.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and the potential for bias in perception-based responses, but the evidence is strong given the use of statistical analyses and the relatively large sample size.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores dairy producers' perceptions of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 and their influence on biosecurity changes. It highlights the challenges producers face in making biosecurity decisions with limited information, balancing guidance, beliefs, and farm constraints. The research aimed to describe perceptions, characterize experiences, identify farm characteristics associated with biosecurity changes, and assess the relationship between perceived biosecurity effectiveness and implementation. A questionnaire was sent to Michigan dairy facilities, achieving a 15.6% response rate. Descriptive statistics and regression analyses were used to evaluate responses. Results showed that 15% of respondents reported confirmed or suspected HPAI on their farms. Among unaffected farms, those with more employees and robotic milking systems were more likely to implement biosecurity changes. The study found that perceived biosecurity effectiveness significantly influenced implementation, with a 24.3 percentage-point difference observed. It also noted that concern about HPAI and perceived farm-level risk played a role in this relationship. The findings suggest that effective communication strategies emphasizing biosecurity practices and presenting HPAI as a manageable threat could support better implementation of biosecurity measures. However, the study's reliance on self-reported data introduces potential bias, limiting the confidence in the results. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the study design and statistical methods used.

title: A GIS-based framework for standardized environmental characterization in One-Health surveillance: a case study of highly pathogenic avian influenza monitoring in Italian wetlands

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the need for integrating environmental factors into the epidemiological interpretation of avian influenza surveillance, as the HPAI panzootic caused by H5 viruses of clade 2.3.4.4b is constantly re-shaping disease ecology in terms of spatio-temporal spread and host spectrum.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A GIS-based framework was developed to standardize environmental characterization of HPAI surveillance sites, specifically implemented at nine wetlands in north-eastern Italy.
analysis.methods: Environmental data were collected using ESRI field map tool, synchronised through ArcGIS online, validated with field-based ground truthing, stored in a spatial relational database, and aggregated into harmonised site-specific descriptors suitable for epidemiological modelling and analyses.
analysis.main_results: The framework produced consistent environmental data and standardized records for each of the nine wetlands in north-eastern Italy.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the utility of the GIS-based framework in standardizing environmental data collection for HPAI surveillance, introducing a novel approach that integrates field ecology with spatial data infrastructures for disease risk analysis.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of standardized environmental surveillance methods for avian influenza, enhancing the accuracy of epidemiological models and supporting more effective disease risk analysis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a specific geographic region and the absence of direct comparisons with other surveillance methods, but the evidence is strong due to the use of validated field data and standardized data management.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a GIS-based framework designed to standardize environmental characterization for highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) surveillance in Italian wetlands. The HPAI panzootic, driven by H5 viruses of clade 2.3.4.4b, has been reshaping disease ecology by altering spatio-temporal spread and host spectrum. The framework was developed to address the need for integrating environmental factors into epidemiological interpretation, as traditional surveillance methods often lack consistent environmental descriptors. Environmental data were collected at nine wetlands in north-eastern Italy using ESRI field map tools and ArcGIS online, validated with field-based ground truthing, and stored in a spatial relational database. The results showed that the framework produced consistent environmental data and standardized records for each site. The authors interpreted these findings as demonstrating the framework's utility in enhancing disease risk analysis by creating a reliable connection between field ecology and spatial data infrastructures. The study's implications suggest that such standardized approaches can improve surveillance and modeling efforts for avian influenza. However, the study is limited by its geographic focus and lack of direct comparisons with other methods, though the evidence is strong due to the rigorous data collection and validation processes.

title: The cow udder as an influenza mixing ground

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate whether the cow udder could serve as a mixing ground for influenza A viruses, particularly in light of the global spread of H5N1 and its ability to infect mammals. This is important because the sustained circulation of H5N1 in dairy cattle raises concerns about its potential for further adaptation and reassortment.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted using bovine-derived cell lines and tissue explants, with a focus on H5N1-infected dairy cattle in the United States. The researchers infected different cow-derived cells with various influenza A virus strains, including avian, human, and swine viruses, to analyze their replication and infection capabilities.
analysis.methods: The researchers used several assays to measure viral replication and compared the fitness of bovine viruses with an avian precursor strain. They also performed co-infection experiments in bovine cells using human and avian influenza strains to assess the potential for co-infection and reassortment.
analysis.main_results: The results showed that mammary cells could be infected by many different influenza A viruses. Additionally, co-infection experiments in bovine cells using human and avian influenza strains produced a cell population infected with both viruses, providing proof of principle for co-infection and reassortment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings support the hypothesis that co-infections of human and avian viruses within the cow mammary glands are possible, thus reassortment events in the cow udder cannot be ruled out.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study highlights the potential role of the cow udder in facilitating viral adaptation and reassortment, which has implications for surveillance and understanding the evolution of influenza A viruses, particularly H5N1, in mammalian hosts.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study has limitations, including the use of cell lines that may lose some bovine characteristics in culture, and the current mass spectrometry analyses only infer possible glycan structures rather than definitively assigning them. Despite these limitations, the evidence is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates whether the cow udder can serve as a mixing ground for influenza A viruses, particularly H5N1, which has been detected in dairy cattle in the United States. The researchers infected bovine-derived cells with various influenza strains, including avian, human, and swine viruses, and found that mammary cells could be easily infected by many different influenza A viruses. Co-infection experiments demonstrated the potential for co-infection and reassortment, supporting the hypothesis that the cow udder may facilitate viral adaptation. The study highlights the importance of understanding this potential role for surveillance and public health, but it has limitations, such as the use of cell lines that may not fully represent bovine tissue characteristics and the reliance on inferred glycan structures from mass spectrometry. The evidence is moderate, as the findings are based on laboratory experiments rather than direct field observations.

analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the need for further validation of AEX-1 cells in large-scale production and the lack of direct comparison with other cell lines in vaccine production.

analysis.summary_en: The study developed AEX-1 cells with enhanced influenza virus replication, showing higher titres of vaccine viruses compared to Vero cells. This suggests AEX-1 cells could improve influenza vaccine production efficiency.

title: Developing and benchmarking one health genomic surveillance tools for influenza A virus in wastewater

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A viruses (IAV) remain a persistent One Health threat, and whole-genome sequencing from wastewater offers a promising surveillance tool.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study benchmarks four targeted enrichment methods suited for multi-subtype whole-genome IAV sequencing, including custom and off-the-shelf methods.
analysis.methods: Ultrafiltration-based virus concentration consistently outperforms large-volume direct extraction across all four sequencing methods, two wastewater matrices, and most spike-in and endogenous virus targets.
analysis.main_results: Our custom HA tiled-amplicon panel is sensitive, fast, and cost-effective, making it suitable for monitoring low-abundance seasonal variants of known subtypes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The custom panel provides needed information for implementing IAV genomic sequencing in routine wastewater surveillance.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of genomic surveillance tools for avian influenza A viruses in wastewater, supporting improved monitoring of low-abundance seasonal variants.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The reliance on conserved and intact primer-binding sites limits primer design to fewer subtypes, and the evidence is based on abstract-only data.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates the effectiveness of four targeted enrichment methods for whole-genome sequencing of influenza A viruses (IAV) in wastewater. The research highlights the challenges of IAV detection in low-abundance environments and introduces a custom HA tiled-amplicon panel as a sensitive, fast, and cost-effective tool for monitoring seasonal variants. The study demonstrates that ultrafiltration-based virus concentration outperforms other methods in wastewater samples. The custom panel is suitable for known subtypes but has limitations due to reliance on conserved primer-binding sites. The findings suggest that these methods can improve genomic surveillance of avian influenza in wastewater, though the evidence is based on abstract-only data. The study contributes to the development of tools for IAV monitoring, emphasizing the importance of tailored approaches for low-abundance variants.
